Q: How should i continue learning java programming A:

If you need to learn data structures and algorithms, you need a book on data structures and algorithms, not on Java (of course you can implement DSA in Java, and there are books on this, but DSA are fundamentally language agnostic). Same for complexity (big O). You may have a look at Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest & Stein, "Introduction to Algorithms", or Sedgewick "Algorithms", or Aho, Hopcroft & Ullman "Data Structures and Algorithms", or Knuth "The Art of Computer Programming". For big O notation and complexity, Sedgewick & Flajolet "Analysis of Algorithms", and Graham, Knuth & Patashnik "Concrete Mathematics".

Q: Value for parameter MessageDeduplicationId is invalid. Reason: The request includes a parameter that is not valid for this queue type A:

Problem occurs because you're trying to send message to a FIFO queue, but you've created a standard queue. Instead of running command:

awslocal sqs create-queue --queue-name QUEUE_NAME

You should run this one (include the FifoQueue attribute):

awslocal sqs create-queue --queue-name QUEUE_NAME --attributes {"FifoQueue":"true"}

Q: How to unescape HTML entities in python A:

How often are new HTML entities being introduced? Who says Python won't maintain that list? Compared to how often will you encounter entities you haven't added to your own list yet, and will need to do so, before it's production ready? What if this needs to run in production autonomously and not just on your own computer under your control, where you could feasibly catch unknown entities and add them?

On the one hand, it's too many entities to load, on the other, it's possibly not enough because it's fixed. Which is it now?

If you really had to deal with documents containing entities not in the HTML 5 spec and you needed to extend that list, you could still import html.entities.html5 and extend that list and use your own matching code. But starting your list from scratch because "you don't need them all" to save a tiny bit of memory is crazy, because it has virtually no detectable advantage but huge practical implications for actually processing documents you don't control.

"Here's your HTML processing application, Mr. Client. We've made sure it saves every KB of memory possible. If you ever encounter unprocessed HTML entities in your data, just let us know the entity names and we'll add them to the list, prepare a new version for you, which you just need to install, and then re-process your documents again. No biggy. Cause we prioritised memory efficiency, you know. And it's not like there's published, standardised lists of well known entities available anyway, right?"

Q: Connecting pyspark cluster installed in an server from another server A:

You can't do that because PySpark alone does not expose any service or endpoint. And anyway to submit Spark jobs, you always need a client.

If you have two machines, just install Spark on one (the server) and PySpark on the other one (the client).

Even though PySpark is a Python client for the Spark engine (overview), the PySpark package comes with its own Spark engine for quickstart, albeit quoting https://pypi.org/project/pyspark/:

This Python packaged version of Spark is suitable for interacting with an existing cluster (be it Spark standalone, YARN) - but does not contain the tools required to set up your own standalone Spark cluster. You can download the full version of Spark from the Apache Spark downloads page.

So basically if you want to do some real work with Spark and PySpark (even on a single machine) it is recommended that you install a Spark engine (as a standalone setup if you don't need YARN). On the Spark server you need to launch master and worker, the PySpark client can access the Spark server at the master's port (usually 7077) with something like this

spark = SparkSession.builder \
    .master("spark://SPARK_SERVER_A_IP:7077") \
    .appName("MyApp") \
    .getOrCreate()

Note that if you don't specify a Spark master, PySpark runs by default in local mode using its built-in Spark engine. If Spark runs on a different server, you need to open port 7077 on the Spark server so the client can connect.

Also very important: if you use an own Spark server make sure that the versions of Spark and PySpark match.
